observation: D'Mello & Graesser's AutoTutor-based body of work found confusion was positively correlated with learning outcomes, while frustration and boredom were negatively correlated, across multiple studies.
claim: Systems should tolerate or even mildly induce confusion rather than back off from it, but should actively intervene on boredom and frustration.
mechanism: Confusion signals productive cognitive disequilibrium that resolves into effortful reasoning and learning; frustration/boredom short-circuit that process.

implications.text: Treat repeated re-reads/dwell spikes (candidate confusion) as 'surface more depth', and idle gaps/rapid dial-flicking (candidate boredom/frustration) as the actual trigger to intervene or offer to stop.

observation: VanLehn's 2011 meta-analysis found step-based intelligent tutoring systems (feedback at each reasoning step) reach effect sizes (~0.76) nearly matching human tutors (~0.79), while answer-based/substep systems perform markedly worse (~0.40).
claim: Granularity of interaction (seeing and responding to intermediate steps), not 'AI vs human,' is the variable that predicts tutoring effectiveness.
mechanism: Fine-grained feedback loops let a system correct or scaffold before an error compounds, mimicking what a human tutor watching over your shoulder would do.

implications.text: Frequent low-stakes feedback loops (Black & Wiliam-style formative signals) are a higher-leverage design lever than any single affect-detection feature.

observation: Bull & Kay's SMILI:) framework classifies open learner models by how much of the model is shown and how much control the user has, and identifies pedagogical (self-assessment) and technical (model-correction) purposes for showing the model.
claim: Letting users see and negotiate with the system's model of them (an open learner model) improves trust and self-regulation.
mechanism: Scrutability lets the user catch and correct a wrong model, and prompts their own reflection on what they know.
context: ITS design literature, taxonomy not RCT

implications.text: Expose 'why you're seeing this' (e.g. 'this expanded because you paused here twice') as a scrutable open learner model, reusing the tree's existing source_span/level metadata.

observation: Niemiec, Sikorski & Walberg's review and later meta-analyses (Karich, Burns & Maki 2014; updated in Review of Educational Research) converge on: average effect of learner control is close to zero, sometimes slightly negative, with control helping confident/skilled learners and hurting less able/novice learners.
claim: Unqualified 'let the user always drive the zoom dial' is not supported; the system should default to steering, especially early or for an unfamiliar topic, and let the user override.
mechanism: Novices lack the metacognitive calibration to navigate wisely without guidance, so open control can lead them to under-challenge themselves or get lost.
population: general students, K-12 through adult (three generations of meta-analysis, 1996-2016)

implications.text: Default to a system-chosen zoom level (e.g. L1) on first open of a document, treating manual dial movement as feedback rather than a decision the system must always defer to.

observation: Cocea & Weibelzahl and Baker et al.'s log-file-analysis line of work models disengagement from raw behavioral logs (dwell time, idle gaps ≥2 minutes) without any webcam/physiological sensing, explicitly noting this is privacy-friendly and equipment-free.
claim: Interaction-log behavior (dwell, re-reads, idle gaps, scroll/zoom patterns) is the right primary signal stack for a single-user local app; webcam/physiological sensing should be deprioritized on privacy/cost grounds.
mechanism: Log-based signals require no extra hardware or biometric capture and are directly generated by the app's own existing instrumentation.
population: mostly K-12 ITS log data (dataset-specific accuracy)

implications.text: Build the signal stack from dwell time, re-visit counts, dial velocity, idle gaps and scroll regressions first; keep webcam/physiological sensing explicitly out of scope for v1.

observation: Multiple papers (Lan & Baraniuk; a Springer 2022 adaptive-curriculum bandit RCT) frame 'which content/format to show next' as a contextual-bandit problem, favored over full RL for cold-start/sparse-reward/non-stationary single-user regimes.
claim: A contextual bandit (not a hand-tuned rule set or full RL) is the right algorithm class for picking presentation variants (zoom level, pre-expansion, section order) per user.
mechanism: Bandits are more sample-efficient than RL and handle the cold-start problem of one user with thin history better than either hand-tuned rules or data-hungry RL.
population: general learners (platform-scale multi-user RCT, not single-user validated)

implications.text: Build the presentation-variant chooser as a contextual bandit seeded with a rule-based prior (e.g. word-count-based L1 target), not a fixed heuristic forever.

observation: People are systematically overconfident about what they understand, especially before being tested (metacomprehension/calibration literature); a CBE-Life Sciences Education study found 2 weeks of structured self-evaluation improved calibration accuracy.
claim: A user's self-report of 'how well do you understand this' is a weaker signal than it sounds and should be triangulated with behavioral signals, not trusted alone.
mechanism: Immediate felt understanding relies on fading surface fluency, not the durable situation-model representation that predicts actual test performance.
population: general students (cognitive psychology literature, large and old)

implications.text: Combine any explicit 'how well do you understand this' probe with implicit behavioral signals (dwell, re-reads) rather than trusting self-report alone.

observation: Contextual-bandit and knowledge-tracing literature structurally implies that with one user and thin history, a naive model either does nothing useful for a long time (cold start) or overfits hard to a single atypical session (e.g. a low-energy day), wrongly learning a permanent preference for the shallowest level.
claim: Riemann must separate a fast-moving 'state today' estimate from a slow-moving 'stable preference' estimate, using decayed/windowed reward averaging, so one bad session doesn't get baked in as a permanent trait.
mechanism: Hierarchical/windowed pooling dampens single-session overfit while still letting the model adapt to genuine long-term preference drift.
population: general recommender-systems practice, generalized to single-user personalization
context: structural/design inference from bandit and recommender-systems literature

implications.text: Store two rolling estimates — a fast session/day-level state and a slow-moving stable preference — and never let one bad day permanently bias the default level.

observation: Explicit feedback (thumbs up/down) is clean but sparse (users rarely bother); implicit feedback (dwell, scroll, re-read, abandonment) is abundant but noisy and ambiguous — standard recommender-systems practice weights explicit feedback more per-observation but relies on implicit for volume and calibration.
claim: Riemann should fuse a sparse explicit thumbs/µEMA signal with abundant implicit interaction-log signal, using the explicit signal to calibrate the implicit model rather than replace it.
mechanism: Explicit feedback is low-noise but too rare to drive minute-to-minute adaptation alone; implicit feedback provides volume but needs periodic explicit anchoring to stay calibrated.
population: general (e-commerce/media recommender-systems practice, generalized to education)

implications.text: A single-tap 'helpful/not helpful' per generated node plus a one-tap mood/energy check-in gives cheap explicit anchors for calibrating the implicit interaction-log model.
